paper.title: Mechanism-Matched Pharmacology of Resistance in EGFR-Mutant NSCLC: Genomic Bypass, Lineage Plasticity, Antibody-Drug Conjugates, and Candidate Biophysical Targets.
paper.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) often responds to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors but develops heterogeneous resistance. This structured narrative review integrates clinical and experimental evidence on resistance after osimertinib and intensified EGFR-directed therapy. It distinguishes on-target EGFR alterations, MET and ERBB-family bypass, downstream signaling, oncogenic fusions, histologic transformation, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, and drug-tolerant persistence, linking each mechanism to an appropriate assay and treatment context. We evaluate next-generation EGFR inhibitors, EGFR-MET combinations, bispecific antibodies, platinum-pemetrexed intensification, and antibody-drug conjugates directed at HER3, TROP2, or HER2. Clinical validation is assessed separately from mechanistic causality, with attention to allelic phase, central nervous system exposure, target engagement, unbound drug concentration, predictive biomarkers, and safety. Ion channels and transporters, including ANO1/TMEM16A, LRRC8/VRAC, KCa3.1, hERG, STIM-ORAI, TRP, and pH regulators, remain exploratory candidate targets. Available evidence for their role in acquired osimertinib resistance is largely indirect; expression or general tumor biology does not establish disease-specific dependency. A mechanism-matched development pathway using paired tissue and plasma sampling, relevant resistant models, causal perturbation, and pharmacodynamic validation is proposed. Clinical decisions should follow validated mechanisms rather than extrapolated biophysical hypotheses.

paper.title: Repurposing of abemaciclib to overcome C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma.
paper.abstract: Background: Acquired resistance to osimertinib mediated by the EGFR C797S mutation remains a major therapeutic challenge in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with limited effective treatment options. This study explored whether abemaciclib, an FDA-approved CDK4/6 inhibitor, can overcome C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Methods: A high-throughput screen of approximately 125,000 compounds was performed using Ba/F3 cells expressing EGFR triple mutations (L858R/T790M/C797S and Del19/T790M/C797S). The impact of abemaciclib on EGFR kinase activity was evaluated via in vitro kinase and Western blot assays. Apoptosis induction was assessed using flow cytometry. The activity of abemaciclib was evaluated using biochemical assays, cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA), molecular docking analyses, CRISPR-engineered isogenic models, xenografts, and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. Results: Abemaciclib was identified as a potent inhibitor of EGFR triple-mutant cell growth and exhibited preferential activity toward mutant EGFR-dependent models. IL-3 rescue assays demonstrated that its antiproliferative effects were dependent on suppression of oncogenic EGFR signaling. Abemaciclib inhibited mutant EGFR kinase activity, reduced EGFR phosphorylation, and induced apoptotic cell death in osimertinib-resistant models while exhibiting substantially weaker activity toward wild-type EGFR. CETSA and molecular docking analyses supported direct engagement of mutant EGFR by abemaciclib. Importantly, abemaciclib significantly suppressed tumor growth in CRISPR-engineered isogenic xenografts and PDX models harboring EGFR C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance. Conclusions: Abemaciclib selectively suppresses C797S-mutant EGFR signaling and demonstrates robust antitumor activity in preclinical models of osimertinib-resistant EGFR-mutant NSCLC. This breakthrough not only overcomes the existing therapeutic barrier but also demonstrates minimal interference with WT EGFR, offering a transformative and precise therapeutic strategy with significant translational and clinical potential. These findings support the therapeutic repurposing of abemaciclib as a potential treatment strategy for EGFR C797S-mediated resistance and provide a translational strategy for overcoming resistance-associated EGFR alterations using clinically available targeted agents.

paper.title: Co-alterations associated with resistance to EGFR inhibitors in advanced EGFR-positive NSCLC: insights from the precision oncology program in two large international real-world cohorts.
paper.abstract: EGFR inhibitors (EGFRi), alone or combined with chemotherapy or bispecific antibodies, are standard first-line therapy for advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC, but their efficacy is limited by heterogeneous resistance mechanisms. To define the impact of genetic co-alterations, we analyzed two complementary real-world cohorts. Patients with EGFR exon 19 deletion or L858R mutations were included from the University Hospital Zurich (USZ; n = 43) and the Flatiron Health-Foundation Medicine clinicogenomic database (FH-FMI CGDB; n = 1927). Duration of treatment (DOT) on first-line EGFRi was assessed in relation to co-alterations at diagnosis. In the FH-FMI CGDB, shorter DOT on osimertinib was associated with co-alterations in ERBB2 (p < 0.01), PIK3CA (p = 0.04), and TP53 (p < 0.01), with similar trends for MET, KRAS, BRAF, and CCNE1. For erlotinib/afatinib, shorter DOT was observed for ERBB2 (p = 0.027) and TP53 (p < 0.01), alongside additional genes. The USZ cohort showed concordant trends. TP53 was the most frequent co-alteration; variants affecting zinc-binding and dimerization domains were associated with shorter DOT. These findings identify co-alterations linked to reduced EGFRi benefit, particularly ERBB2, PIK3CA, and TP53, and highlight residue-specific TP53 effects. This supports comprehensive genomic profiling and function-based stratification to refine treatment strategies in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.

paper.title: Osimertinib, platinum, and etoposide for patients with metastatic EGFR/TP53/RB1-mutant lung cancers at risk for histological transformation.
paper.abstract: Although EGFR inhibitors are highly effective for treating EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinomas (EGFR+ LUADs), resistance inevitably emerges, with histologic transformation to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) representing a particularly aggressive mechanism. Our prospective trial enrolled patients with EGFR+ LUAD at high risk of transformation (TP53/RB1-deficient) and treated them with first-line osimertinib combined with platinum and etoposide. Despite the addition of SCLC-directed chemotherapy, nearly half of patients (5 of 11) underwent SCLC transformation, with median progression-free survival of 11 months and overall survival of 33 months. Genomic and single-cell transcriptomic profiling of patient samples revealed clinical and subclinical plasticity associated with TP53/RB1 comutations, including histological transformation to SCLC, as well as mesenchymal and squamous histologies. These changes in plasticity were linked to progressive disruption of the RB pathway, leading to altered chromatin accessibility and induction of neuronal differentiation and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition transcriptional programs, further intensified by osimertinib treatment. These findings provide insights into the role of plasticity in mediating drug tolerance.

paper.title: Coexistence of Osimertinib-Resistant and Osimertinib-Sensitive cell states in an EGFR-Mutant NSCLC model derived at osimertinib resistance.
paper.abstract: Background: Osimertinib is a standard first-line treatment for EGFR-mutant Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC), but acquired resistance remains a clinical challenge. Resistance involves genetic mechanisms and non-genetic cell-state transitions, including epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) plasticity and drug-tolerant persister phenotypes. Patient-derived models established at disease progression may better capture clinically relevant resistance mechanisms. Methods: We established LIBM-ADK-11 from the pleural effusion of a patient with EGFR exon 19p.Leu747_Pro753delinsSer-mutant NSCLC progressing on osimertinib. Cells were studied at low and high passages and fractionated by CD44 expression into CD44-positive/P2 and CD44-negative/P4 subpopulations. EGFR mutation status, CD44 expression, transcriptomics, growth, osimertinib sensitivity, EGFR signaling, sphere formation, cell-cycle distribution and pemetrexed response were evaluated. Results: LIBM-ADK-11 retained the EGFR mutation during long-term culture. CD44 sorting identified two phenotypically distinct cell states. CD44-positive P2 cells were enriched for extracellular matrix remodeling, EMT-like, inflammatory, CAF-like and macrophage/TAM-mimicry programs, with increased glycolysis-related signatures, slower growth, higher metabolic activity and osimertinib resistance. CD44-negative P4 cells displayed a more epithelial profile, cholesterol-associated gene expression and greater osimertinib sensitivity. Osimertinib inhibited EGFR phosphorylation in both populations, indicating that P2 resistance was not explained by persistent EGFR signaling. Long-term culture favored loss of CD44-positive cells, whereas osimertinib delayed this loss and preferentially depleted the CD44-negative fraction. Pemetrexed partially reduced both compartments. Conclusions: LIBM-ADK-11 is a clinically relevant model of osimertinib-resistant EGFR-mutant NSCLC in which CD44-positive drug-tolerant and CD44-negative drug-sensitive states coexist. These findings highlight phenotypic heterogeneity as a potential determinant of osimertinib resistance and support strategies addressing distinct cellular states at disease progression.

paper.title: Pterostilbene enhances Osimertinib sensitivity in non-small cell lung cancer through FGFR4-dependent ferroptosis.
paper.abstract: Background: Osimertinib is a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has become a mainstay treatment for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, acquired resistance develops in most patients and ultimately compromises durable clinical benefit. Therefore, effective combination strategies to enhance Osimertinib sensitivity and delay or overcome resistance remain an urgent unmet clinical need. Methods: The antitumor effects of pterostilbene in combination with Osimertinib were evaluated in EGFR-mutant and osimertinib-resistant NSCLC cell lines using CCK-8, colony formation, EdU incorporation, wound healing, and Transwell invasion assays. In vivo efficacy and safety were evaluated in nude mouse xenograft models. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, ferroptosis-related biochemical parameters, protein expression profiles, and transcriptomic profiles were analyzed. The involvement of ferroptosis and FGFR4 signaling was further validated using the ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) and FGFR4 siRNA-mediated knockdown. Results: Pterostilbene markedly potentiated the antitumor efficacy of Osimertinib in vitro and in vivo and restored drug responsiveness in Osimertinib-resistant NSCLC cells. Mechanistically, the combination induced ferroptosis, as indicated by enhanced lipid peroxidation, intracellular Fe2+ accumulation, and reduced expression of key ferroptosis-protective proteins, including GPX4 and xCT. Consistently, pharmacological inhibition of ferroptosis attenuated the antitumor effects of the combination. Furthermore, combined treatment modulated FGFR4-associated ERK/AKT signaling and disrupted redox and iron homeostasis. FGFR4 depletion significantly attenuated ferroptosis induction and reduced the synergistic anticancer effects of the combination, whereas FGFR4 re-expression restored treatment responsiveness, supporting an FGFR4-dependent therapeutic response. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that pterostilbene enhances the antitumor efficacy of Osimertinib through the induction of FGFR4-dependent ferroptosis, providing mechanistic insights and suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy to overcome EGFR-TKI resistance in NSCLC.

paper.title: Centromere-Targeting Chimeras for Combating Cancer Drug Resistance.
paper.abstract: Centromere protein B (CENPB), the only sequence-specific DNA-binding protein at centromeres, maintains chromosomal stability and accurate mitotic segregation. Its overexpression in aggressive cancers is associated with aneuploidy and poor prognosis, yet CENPB remains therapeutically underexplored because direct inhibitors are unavailable. Here, we develop CENPB OligoTAC, a DNA-based PROTAC comprising a CENPB-binding oligodeoxynucleotide linked to an E3 ligase ligand. CENPB OligoTAC induces ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of CENPB, disrupting centromere integrity, causing chromosome mis-segregation, and activating apoptosis. It shows potent activity in preclinical non-small cell lung cancer models resistant to first-, second-, and third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors, while exhibiting minimal cytotoxicity toward normal cells and good serum stability. In vivo, CENPB OligoTAC demonstrates favorable pharmacokinetics, good tolerability, and no significant hematological changes. By exploiting cancer cells' dependence on centromeric stability, this platform offers a novel strategy for selectively targeting aneuploid malignancies.

paper.title: Prolonged survival after small-cell transformation of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma: a case report.
paper.abstract: Transformed small cell lung cancer (T-SCLC) is most commonly observed in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma and represents an important mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs). Its reported clinical incidence is approximately 3%-10%. Patients with T-SCLC often experience rapid disease progression and poor overall prognosis, and no established standard treatment regimen is currently available. We report a case of advanced EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with RB1, TP53, and BRCA2 co-mutations that underwent small-cell transformation during treatment. Small-cell transformation was detected through close surveillance and confirmed by repeat biopsy. The patient subsequently received individualized multimodal therapy, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and local radiotherapy, and remained alive 43 months after the initial diagnosis.

paper.title: Patterns of Treatment and Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Stage 1/2 EGFR-mutated Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Treated With Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy: A Global, Multicenter, Retrospective Study.
paper.abstract: Purpose: We report clinical outcomes, mutation testing patterns, and treatment patterns from a global, real-world, retrospective, observational study in patients with stage 1/2 epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Methods and materials: Data were extracted from medical records of adults with stage 1/2 EGFR-mutated NSCLC (diagnosed January 2016-December 2019), who underwent stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) as standard of care. The primary objective was assessment of real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS). Secondary objectives included assessment of mutation testing patterns, treatment sequencing post-SBRT, real-world time to next treatment or death (rwTTNTD), and real-world overall survival (rwOS). Results: Data were extracted from medical records of 82 patients across six countries; 66% of patients had medically inoperable tumors; 43% had tumors harboring exon 19 deletion (Ex19del), 55% had L858R, 1% had both Ex19del and L858R, and 1% had L858R and an exon 20 insertion. Overall, 91% of patients had stage 1A/1B disease and 9% had stage 2A/2B. All patients underwent SBRT as standard of care; 31 patients (38%) progressed following SBRT. Of patients who received subsequent treatment (n = 25), most received EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs; 88%; n = 22/25); first-/second-generation EGFR-TKIs n=17, third-generation EGFR-TKIs n=5. Median (95% confidence interval [CI]) rwPFS, rwTTNTD, and rwOS were 47.1 (38.7-57.8), 49.8 (40.7-not estimable [NE]), and 62.9 (50.8-NE) months, respectively. The rwPFS rates at 12, 24, 36, 48, and 60 months (95% CI) were 90% (81-95), 76% (65-84), 65% (53-74), 48% (35-60), and 34% (19-48), respectively. Conclusions: In this global, real-world, retrospective study in patients with stage 1/2 EGFR-mutated NSCLC who underwent SBRT, the majority of whom had medically inoperable tumors, the 4-year rwPFS rate was <50%. Further studies are needed to confirm the potential role for EGFR-TKI therapy in this setting.

paper.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis and progression of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with activating mutations serving as key determinants of sensitivity to targeted therapies. The prevalence and spectrum of EGFR mutations are influenced by histology, ethnicity, and environmental factors, encompassing common alterations such as exon 19 deletions and the L858R point mutation, as well as uncommon variants including exon 20 insertions, kinase domain duplications, and other rare substitutions. These molecular distinctions underlie differential responses to first-, second-, and third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), emphasizing the necessity of precise molecular profiling for individualized treatment selection. Although EGFR TKIs initially produce robust responses, resistance inevitably develops via on-target mutations (e.g., T790M, C797S), activation of bypass signaling pathways, co-occurring genetic alterations, and histologic or phenotypic transformation, challenging long-term disease control. Contemporary strategies to overcome resistance include combination therapies integrating TKIs with MEK, MET, or AXL inhibitors, antibody-based therapeutics, bispecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, and emerging multifunctional biologics. Additionally, immunomodulatory interventions and nanotechnology-based delivery systems enhance anti-tumor efficacy while mitigating resistance. Non-invasive monitoring techniques, such as liquid biopsies, circulating tumor DNA profiling, and advanced imaging modalities, enable longitudinal assessment of mutation dynamics and therapeutic response, informing adaptive, precision-guided treatment strategies. This review synthesizes current knowledge on EGFR mutations, resistance mechanisms, and emerging therapeutic approaches in NSCLC, highlighting the integration of molecular, immunologic, and technological modalities to improve patient outcomes and advance precision oncology.
